mcqs.question: Why does `git status` get noticeably slower in a repository with a million files, even if only one file changed?
options: git status re-downloads the full object history on every call
It must stat every file in the working tree to detect what changed, and that cost scales with total file count
git status only slows down if the changed file is very large
It re-runs garbage collection before reporting status
mcqs.explanation: Detecting changes means comparing the working tree against the index file by file, so the cost scales with how many files exist on disk, regardless of how many actually changed. It doesn't re-download history or trigger gc, and the slowdown is about file count, not any one file's size.

mcqs.question: A CI job only needs the latest commit to run a build — it never needs history. Which clone strategy is the best fit?
options: A full clone, since CI environments should always have complete history
Sparse checkout only, leaving history untouched
Partial clone with lazy blob fetching
A shallow clone with `--depth 1`, since older history is irrelevant here
mcqs.explanation: When only the latest state matters and history is never queried, a shallow clone directly minimizes what's transferred by skipping older commits entirely. A full clone wastes bandwidth on unneeded history, sparse checkout alone doesn't address history size, and partial clone solves a different problem — lazy content fetching across a full commit graph.

mcqs.question: In a thousand-engineer monorepo, why is a CODEOWNERS file preferred over relying on engineers to know who to ask for review?
options: It's required by git itself for any PR to be mergeable
It automatically fixes merge conflicts in owned paths
It makes review routing explicit and machine-enforced, since no one can personally track ownership across thousands of possible reviewers
It replaces the need for any human code review entirely
mcqs.explanation: At real scale, tribal knowledge of "who owns this directory" doesn't hold up, so mapping paths to owners and enforcing it automatically is what keeps reviews routed correctly. CODEOWNERS isn't a git requirement, doesn't touch conflict resolution, and still requires actual human reviewers — it only automates who gets asked.

mcqs.question: Why can't an unsigned commit's author field be trusted as proof of who actually wrote it?
options: Unsigned commits don't record an author field at all
The author name and email are just local git config values that anyone can set to anything
Unsigned commits are rejected by all major git hosting platforms
The author field is only populated after a commit is pushed
mcqs.explanation: user.name and user.email are plain local configuration, freely settable to any value, so an unsigned commit's claimed authorship carries no cryptographic guarantee — only a GPG signature actually proves who created it. Author fields are recorded at commit time regardless of signing, and unsigned commits aren't universally rejected by hosting platforms.

mcqs.question: A 50-engineer team with a small, low-history repository is considering adopting sparse checkout and partial clone tooling. What's the most likely outcome?
options: Meaningful performance gains proportional to the tooling investment
Added operational complexity with little benefit, since their repo isn't large enough for the underlying problem to exist yet
Guaranteed reduced CI cost regardless of repo size
A requirement to migrate to a monorepo structure first
mcqs.explanation: Scale tooling pays for itself once cloning and checkout are genuinely slow — a small repo doesn't have that problem, so the added configuration and maintenance surface outweighs any benefit. Gains aren't guaranteed independent of repo size, CI cost isn't automatically reduced, and none of this tooling requires a monorepo migration.

mcqs.question: A 2GB file was committed by accident and deleted in the very next commit. What's true about the repository's clone size going forward?
options: The clone size returns to normal immediately since the file no longer exists in the latest commit
The file only affects clone size until the next `git gc` runs
The blob remains part of history and every future clone still transfers it, unless history is explicitly rewritten to remove it
Git automatically detects and strips deleted large files during clone
mcqs.explanation: Deleting a file in a later commit only removes it from that commit's tree — the blob is still reachable from the earlier commit and stays part of history permanently, transferred on every clone, until a tool like filter-repo or BFG explicitly rewrites history to remove it. Neither gc nor clone strips reachable objects automatically, regardless of file size.
